We address two issues in the thermodynamic model for nuclear disassembly. Surprisingly large differences in results for specific heat were seen in predictions from the canonical and grand canonical ensembles when the nuclear system passes from liquid-gas co-existence to the pure gas phase. We are able to pinpoint and understand the reasons for such and other discrepancies when they appear. There is a subtle but important difference in the physics addressed in the two models. In particular if we reformulate the parameters in the canonical model to better approximate the physics addressed in the grand canonical model, calculations for observables converge. Next we turn to the issue of bimodality in the probability distribution of the largest fragment in both canonical and grand canonical ensembles. We demonstrate that this distribution is very closely related to average multiplicities. The relationship of the bimodal distribution to phase transition is discussed.

# Ensemble Discrepancies in Specific Heat and Bimodality in Nuclear Fragmentation

## Overview

This study investigates surprisingly large discrepancies in specific heat predictions between the canonical and grand canonical ensembles as a nuclear system transitions from the liquid-gas co-existence region into the pure gas phase. While statistical ensembles are generally expected to yield equivalent thermodynamic results in the appropriate limits, the observed differences in this transitional regime are substantial enough to warrant a detailed investigation into their physical origins.

## Identifying the Source of the Discrepancies

A central contribution of this work is the identification and explanation of the underlying reasons for these discrepancies. Rather than attributing the differences to numerical artifacts or computational limitations, the authors trace them to a subtle but physically important distinction in the problems that the two models actually address. The canonical and grand canonical formulations, despite their formal similarities, impose different constraints on the system—most notably regarding particle number conservation—and it is precisely this difference that becomes pronounced when the system approaches the pure gas phase.

## Reconciling the Two Ensembles

To demonstrate that these discrepancies are indeed rooted in the differing physical assumptions rather than in any fundamental inconsistency, the authors reformulate the parameters of the canonical model so that it more closely approximates the physics captured by the grand canonical framework. When the models are placed on equivalent physical footing in this way, the calculations for the relevant observables are shown to converge. This convergence confirms the proposed explanation and reinforces the importance of carefully matching the physical conditions when comparing predictions across different statistical ensembles.

## Bimodality in the Largest-Fragment Distribution

Building on this analysis, the paper examines bimodality in the probability distribution of the largest fragment within both the canonical and grand canonical ensembles. Bimodality—the appearance of two distinct peaks in the probability distribution—has attracted considerable interest as a potential signature of phase transitions in finite nuclear systems, and its study within complementary ensemble descriptions provides a more complete understanding of the phenomenon.

## Connection to Multiplicities and Phase Transitions

Finally, the authors demonstrate that this bimodal distribution is closely related to the average multiplicities of the system. By establishing this relationship, they clarify how the structure of the largest-fragment distribution reflects the broader fragmentation behavior of the system. The discussion further explores the connection between bimodality and phase transitions, highlighting the physical significance of these observations for characterizing the nuclear liquid-gas transition.

# Specific Heat Discrepancies Between Canonical and Grand Canonical Ensembles in Nuclear Disassembly Models

## Introduction

The statistical description of nuclear multifragmentation has long relied on thermodynamic models that treat an excited nucleus as a system capable of breaking apart into a distribution of fragments. Among the theoretical frameworks employed for this purpose, the canonical and grand canonical ensembles are the most widely used. In principle, these two ensembles should yield equivalent physical predictions in the thermodynamic limit. In practice, however, they differ in their treatment of conserved quantities: the canonical ensemble fixes the total number of nucleons, whereas the grand canonical ensemble allows particle number to fluctuate around an average value fixed by a chemical potential. This distinction becomes particularly important when studying finite systems and when calculating observables that are sensitive to fluctuations, such as the specific heat.

## Motivation

This study focuses on the discrepancies that arise in the predictions of specific heat between the canonical and grand canonical ensembles within the thermodynamic model for nuclear disassembly. These discrepancies are especially pronounced in the region corresponding to the transition from a mixed liquid-gas phase to a pure gas phase. The specific heat is a key thermodynamic observable in the identification of phase transitions, since features such as peaks or divergences in its temperature dependence are often interpreted as signatures of critical behavior. Understanding why the two ensembles diverge in their predictions is therefore essential for a reliable interpretation of experimental multifragmentation data.

## Methodology

To address this problem, we introduce a reformulation of the parameters used in the canonical model so that they are more consistent with the underlying physics of the grand canonical framework. Rather than treating the canonical parameters as fixed inputs, we recast them in a way that respects the statistical assumptions inherent to the grand canonical description, in which the system exchanges particles with a reservoir. This reformulation provides a controlled means of comparing the two ensembles on common physical footing and of isolating the origin of the discrepancies in the computed specific heat.

## Results

The analysis demonstrates that once the canonical parameters are reformulated in this manner, the calculated observables from the two ensembles converge. This convergence indicates that the apparent disagreement between the ensembles originates largely from an inconsistent choice of parameters rather than from a fundamental difference in the physics they describe. When placed on equivalent grounds, both frameworks yield compatible thermodynamic behavior across the transition region.

Furthermore, the study reveals a close relationship between the bimodal distribution of the largest fragment and the average multiplicities of the disassembling system. Bimodality in the size distribution of the largest fragment is frequently regarded as a robust signal of a first-order-like phase transition, since it reflects the coexistence of two distinct system configurations—one dominated by a large residual fragment and one characterized by fragmentation into many smaller pieces. The correlation between this bimodal behavior and the average multiplicities links a fluctuation-based observable to a more conventional average quantity, strengthening their combined diagnostic value.

## Conclusion

By reconciling the canonical and grand canonical predictions through a physically motivated reformulation of parameters, this work clarifies the origin of specific heat discrepancies in the thermodynamic model of nuclear disassembly. The demonstrated connection between the bimodal distribution of the largest fragment and average multiplicities offers additional insight into the nature of the liquid-gas to pure gas phase transition in finite nuclear systems, and supports the use of these observables as complementary indicators of phase-transition signatures in multifragmentation studies.

# An Unexpected Journey

**Surprisingly**, the path I had walked past a hundred times held a secret I never noticed. For years, I hurried along that same street, my mind occupied with deadlines and worries, never once pausing to look beyond the familiar rows of buildings.

**There**, tucked between an old bookstore and a quiet café, stood a narrow doorway I had somehow always overlooked. It was painted a faded blue, with ivy creeping along its frame and a small brass handle worn smooth by countless hands. How had I missed something so charming for all this time?

Curiosity finally got the better of me. I pushed the door open and stepped inside, discovering a hidden garden filled with blooming flowers, chirping birds, and a stillness that seemed to belong to another world entirely. The noise of the city faded away, replaced by the gentle sound of a trickling fountain.

**Next**, I plan to return with a book and spend an entire afternoon in that peaceful sanctuary. This little adventure taught me an important lesson: sometimes the most remarkable discoveries are waiting right in front of us, hidden in plain sight. All we need to do is slow down, open our eyes, and stay curious about the ordinary world around us.

You never know what wonders might be just one unopened door away.

# Abstract

We present a comparative study of canonical and grand canonical ensembles within the thermodynamic model of nuclear multifragmentation, focusing on the disassembly of an excited nuclear system into fragments of various sizes. While both ensembles are expected to yield equivalent results in the thermodynamic limit, we demonstrate that significant discrepancies emerge for finite nuclear systems, particularly in observables sensitive to fluctuations. Our calculations reveal that the specific heat exhibits notable differences between the two ensembles in the vicinity of the liquid-gas phase transition, where the canonical treatment—which conserves the total number of nucleons—produces a sharper peak and enhanced signatures of the phase transition compared to the grand canonical formulation. We further investigate the probability distribution of the largest fragment size, which serves as an order parameter for the transition. The canonical ensemble displays a clear bimodal structure in this distribution near the transition temperature, reflecting the coexistence of ordered (liquid-like) and disordered (gas-like) configurations, whereas the grand canonical ensemble tends to wash out or modify this bimodal signal due to particle-number fluctuations. We analyze the origin of these differences in terms of constraints imposed by mass conservation and finite-size effects, and discuss the implications for interpreting experimental multifragmentation data. Our results underscore the importance of choosing an appropriate statistical framework when extracting thermodynamic signatures of the nuclear liquid-gas phase transition from finite systems.

Statistical models have proven remarkably successful in describing the fragmentation of excited nuclear systems formed in intermediate-energy heavy-ion collisions. While the grand canonical ensemble has been widely employed due to its analytical tractability, its applicability to finite nuclear systems—where particle number is strictly conserved and fluctuations are non-negligible—warrants careful scrutiny. We show that ensemble equivalence is recovered only in the thermodynamic limit, and we quantify the deviations as a function of system size. # Abstract

Statistical multifragmentation models provide a framework for understanding the nuclear liquid-gas phase transition observed in intermediate-energy heavy-ion collisions. However, thermodynamic observables computed within different statistical ensembles can diverge significantly near the transition, reflecting the finite size of nuclear systems where ensemble equivalence breaks down. We examine two related signatures of this transition.

**Specific heat and ensemble inequivalence.** In macroscopic systems all ensembles yield identical thermodynamics, but for finite nuclei the canonical and grand canonical descriptions differ markedly near the liquid-gas coexistence region. The grand canonical ensemble, which allows particle-number fluctuations, tends to smooth the transition and can suppress or eliminate the negative specific heat that arises in more constrained ensembles. In the microcanonical and canonical treatments, the fixed conserved quantities (energy and/or mass) permit anomalous convex intruders in the entropy, producing a backbending caloric curve and a negative branch in the specific heat—a hallmark of a first-order transition in finite systems. The magnitude and even the sign of the specific heat near the transition therefore depend on which fluctuations the ensemble permits, making ensemble choice a physically meaningful, not merely technical, consideration when comparing to data.

**Bimodality of the largest fragment.** A complementary and more directly observable signal is the bimodal distribution of the size (or charge) of the largest fragment produced in each event. Near the transition, the system fluctuates between a "liquid-like" configuration dominated by a single large residue and a "gas-like" configuration of many small fragments, yielding a two-peaked order-parameter distribution. This bimodality is thermodynamically linked to the convexity of the entropy and hence to the negative specific heat discussed above; the depth of the distribution's minimum reflects the interfacial free-energy cost of phase coexistence. Because bimodality is accessible in event-by-event experimental data, it offers a robust and model-independent indicator of the first-order character of the nuclear liquid-gas transition, while remaining sensitive to the ensemble and sorting conditions under which fragmentation events are selected.

---

# Abstract

The thermodynamic modeling of nuclear multifragmentation continues to face persistent theoretical challenges concerning the statistical interpretation of breakup observables. In this work, we address two outstanding problems within the canonical framework of the statistical multifragmentation model. First, we investigate the convergence behavior of physical observables under alternative parameterizations of the canonical ensemble. We demonstrate that reformulating the model in terms of intensive control variables introduces subtle inconsistencies in the calculation of fragment size distributions and thermodynamic potentials, which have historically obscured comparisons between competing formulations. By deriving the appropriate transformation relations between parameter sets, we establish the conditions under which observables converge to a unique, physically meaningful limit, and we quantify the systematic errors that arise when these conditions are violated. Second, we examine the widely invoked association between bimodality in the fragment-size or energy distributions and the presence of a first-order phase transition in finite nuclear systems. Through explicit canonical calculations across the coexistence region, we clarify the circumstances under which bimodal signatures genuinely reflect a phase transition, as opposed to arising from finite-size effects, constraint ensembles, or the choice of order parameter. Our results reconcile previously conflicting reports in the literature and provide a rigorous criterion linking the curvature anomalies of the microcanonical entropy to the emergence of bimodal probability distributions. These findings offer a consistent thermodynamic foundation for interpreting experimental multifragmentation data and sharpen the diagnostic use of bimodality as a signal of the nuclear liquid-gas phase transition.
